sheets.name: Park Güell
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Eusebi Güell
sheets.timeline: Commissioned 1900 as a private residential development; built 1900-1914 (works abandoned with only 2 of 60 planned houses built); sold by Güell's heirs to Barcelona City Council in 1922; opened as a municipal park in 1926; declared an artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
sheets.inspiration: Inspired by the English garden-city movement (hence the English word 'Park' in its name); marks Gaudí's 'naturalist period', in which his study of nature and organic forms drove both ornament and underlying structural geometry. Symbolic references throughout include political Catalanism (entrance stairway) and Catholicism (the Calvary, originally conceived as a chapel).
sheets.construction_process: Built 1900-1914 as a failed private residential estate (60 triangular plots planned, only 2 houses built) before being abandoned and later purchased by the City Council.
technical_facts: Uses inverted catenary arches for its viaducts and elevated pathways, the same load-bearing-compression method Gaudí used earlier at Colònia Güell.
Entry to the Monumental Zone (main terrace, mosaics, viaducts, gate area) has required a paid ticket since October 2013; Barcelona residents enter free.
artistic_facts: UNESCO's 1984 inscription describes the park's architecture as combining the Arts and Crafts movement, Symbolism, Expressionism, and Rationalism, and as having presaged techniques of 20th-century Modernism.
Introduced curved, undulating benches at Park Güell -- a precursor to the style Gaudí later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as Casa Milà.
Catenary/compression structural logic shared with the Espai Gaudí attic at Casa Milà, though executed in stone viaducts here versus brick vaulting there.

sheets.name: The Dragon / Salamander (El Drac)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the main terrace/entrance works, documented as complete by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description of the site.
sheets.inspiration: Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery, though sources disagree on whether the figure represents a dragon or a salamander -- the official park site itself uses both terms.
sheets.construction_process: A curved masonry/mortar core was built up first, then clad in small, irregular ceramic trencadís fragments (rather than flat tiles) so the mosaic skin could conform to the compound curvature without cracking.
technical_facts: Functions as the overflow spout of the park's rainwater system: water falling on the Greek Theatre/Nature Square above is collected by a conduit inside the Hypostyle Room's colonnade and channeled to an underground cistern, with the dragon's mouth as that system's overflow outlet.
artistic_facts: Covered in trencadís (tile-shard mosaic); the official park site calls it 'the most popular image of the park.'
Sits on the Dragon Stairway, a twin flight of steps divided into three landings: goblin-like shapes on the first landing, the emblem of Catalonia on the second, and the dragon/salamander further up.
general_knowledge_facts: Popularly associated with mythological guardian-dragon imagery (e.g. the dragon of the Garden of the Hesperides) -- a widely repeated interpretation, not confirmed by any Gaudí-authored source.
similarities: Trencadís cladding technique shared with the rooftop chimneys of Casa Milà and with the serpentine bench in this same park.

sheets.name: Laundry Room Portico (Pòrtic de la Bugaderia)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Part of the original park infrastructure built 1900-1914.
sheets.inspiration: Described by the park's own site as taking 'the shape of a great wave atop slanting columns' -- called one of the finest examples of Gaudí's organic architecture; the slanted double colonnade evokes a stone forest, echoing how the park's viaduct columns and vaults elsewhere mimic tree trunks and natural forms.
sheets.construction_process: Built from unworked stone taken from the same hillside it stands on, so the structure visually grows out of the mountain rather than sitting on top of it.
technical_facts: The double colonnade of slanting columns acts as a structural buttress against the retaining wall behind it -- the tilt is load-bearing, not decorative.

Uses the same structural logic as the park's viaducts: inclined stone columns form a parabola/inverted-catenary profile so the columns work in pure compression along the line of thrust, without needing external buttressing.
similarities: Shares its inclined-column, inverted-catenary compression logic with the viaducts in this same park and, in brick-vault form, with the Espai Gaudí attic at Casa Milà.
_notes: Check: no image folder of its own in the supplied landmark list for this element -- confirm whether one exists or whether its images are spread across other folders.

sheets.name: Porter's Lodge (entrance gatehouses)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built early in the 1900-1914 construction phase; documented as already constructed by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description.
sheets.inspiration: Whimsical, fairy-tale-like pavilion forms marking the park's main entrance, reflecting Güell's ambition to recreate an English residential-park model.
technical_facts: One of the two pavilions originally housed a phone booth; the other now contains a permanent exhibit of the Barcelona City History Museum.
artistic_facts: Forms a pair of gatehouses flanking the park's main entrance, among the first structures built on site.

sheets.name: Serpentine Bench (Banc Serpentejant)
sheets.creator: Josep Maria Jujol (design of the trencadís bench, under Gaudí's overall project)
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the main terrace works during the 1900-1914 construction phase; the terrace and its hypostyle support were already in use for events by 1907.
sheets.inspiration: Its ergonomic, curving form creates enclaves along its length that encourage social interaction rather than facing visitors outward in a straight line.
sheets.construction_process: Long, curving bench shaped like a sea serpent, bordering the terrace above the Hypostyle Room, clad in trencadís mosaic.
technical_facts: Sits directly atop the Hypostyle Room's vaulted terrace, following the ergonomic curve designed to double as a shared social space rather than a simple boundary wall.
artistic_facts: One of Gaudí's introductions of curved, undulating bench forms at Park Güell, a precursor to the style he later fully realized at the Sagrada Família.
similarities: Trencadís technique shared with the dragon in this same park and with the rooftop chimneys of Casa Milà.
Design attributed to Jujol, like the interior wrought-iron gate in the Casa Milà courtyards.

sheets.name: Hypostyle Room (Room of a Hundred Columns)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Documented as fully covered/completed by 1907, when events were already being held in the great square above it; the tiled bench that borders the terrace above was completed in 1914.
sheets.inspiration: The vaulted colonnade's mosaic-decorated ceiling recalls grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.
sheets.construction_process: A forest of columns forming a vaulted space that structurally supports the great terrace and serpentine bench above it.
technical_facts: Functions as part of the park's rainwater collection system: a conduit inside the colonnade gathers water falling on the terrace above and channels it to an underground cistern, ultimately overflowing through the dragon's mouth.
artistic_facts: Ceiling mosaics recall grotesque motifs inspired by Roman architecture, particularly the Domus Aurea.
similarities: Structurally supports the serpentine bench on the terrace above, and feeds the water system that exits through the dragon.

sheets.name: Viaducts / elevated pathways
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built during the 1900-1914 construction phase; documented as partly complete (viaducts and part of the great esplanade) by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description.
sheets.inspiration: Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, blending the paths seamlessly with the surrounding landscape.
sheets.construction_process: A system of elevated pathways, originally intended for carriages, built from local stone using inclined columns and vaulted supports that follow the natural lie of the land.
technical_facts: As with Gaudí's earlier work at Colònia Güell, the viaducts use inverted catenary arches to achieve optimal load-bearing compression, so the stone columns work in pure compression without needing external buttressing.
artistic_facts: Columns and vaulted supports mimic tree trunks and natural forms, part of Gaudí's naturalist-period design language for the park.
similarities: Shares its inclined-column, inverted-catenary compression logic with the Laundry Room Portico in this same park and, in brick-vault form, with the Espai Gaudí attic at Casa Milà.

sheets.name: Gaudí House Museum (the former show home)
sheets.creator: Francesc Berenguer i Mestres (architect of the house); lived in by Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built in 1904 as the show home of the failed 60-plot residential development; it never sold; Gaudí bought it with his savings and moved in during 1906 with his father and his niece; became the Gaudí House Museum in 1963; declared a national monument in 1969.
sheets.inspiration: Originally conceived as a sample of the English 'garden city' model that Eusebi Güell wanted to sell to Barcelona's upper middle class.
sheets.construction_process: One of only two houses ever built out of the sixty planned triangular plots; when it failed to sell, Güell persuaded Gaudí to buy it.
general_knowledge_facts: It is the only one of the project's show homes not designed by Gaudí himself, but by his collaborator Francesc Berenguer i Mestres.
similarities: Shares the failed-residential-development origin of Park Güell with the rest of the park's infrastructure (the viaducts and the Laundry Room Portico).

sheets.name: Hill of the Three Crosses (El Turó de les Tres Creus)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built during the 1900-1914 construction phase, at the highest point of the park.
sheets.inspiration: The project's Catholic reference, originally conceived as a chapel; it symbolises the Christian Calvary.
sheets.construction_process: A stairway climbing to the top of the hill, crowned by three stone crosses.
artistic_facts: One of the three crosses points to the sky; the other two mark the cardinal points.
From this point you can see the Sagrada Família, the Torre Glòries, Montjuïc and the Mediterranean.
similarities: The park's Catholic religious reference, paralleling the political Catalanist symbolism of the entrance stairway in the same park.

sheets.name: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Pere Milà and Roser Segimon
sheets.timeline: Commissioned September 1905; presented to Barcelona City Council February 1906; pre-existing building demolished and construction begun 1906; completed December 1910; certificate of completion issued October 1912; declared a historic/artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984; headquarters of Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera since 2013.

technical_figures.Storeys: 9 (basement, ground floor, mezzanine, main/noble floor, four upper floors, attic)

sheets.inspiration: Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa.
sheets.purpose: Built as a mixed-use apartment block: the Milà family lived on the noble floor and the four upper floors were let as rental apartments, over a ground floor and basement designed for vehicle access. It stopped being a private residence when it was taken over for other uses, and since 2013 it has served as a cultural centre and the headquarters of the Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, open to visitors.
materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, lower floor; Villefranche quarry, upper floors)
sheets.construction_process: Gaudí's last private residence commission; the pre-existing building on the plot was demolished (unlike the Casa Batlló renovation) and the new self-supporting stone facade, connected to curved iron floor beams, was built 1906-1910.
technical_facts: Self-supporting stone facade with no load-bearing walls, connected to curved iron beams surrounding the perimeter of each floor -- allowing interior walls to be added or removed without affecting the building's stability.

In August 1908 the City Council fined the project for exceeding its permitted height and site boundaries; the dispute was resolved in December 1909 when the building was certified as monumental and exempted from strict bylaw compliance.
artistic_facts: Nicknamed 'La Pedrera' ('the stone quarry') by residents who disliked its rough-hewn, undulating stone facade -- an insult that became its popular name.
Considered a predecessor of later biomorphic buildings such as the 1921 Einstein Tower (Erich Mendelsohn), the Guggenheim Museum (Frank Wright), and Frank Gehry's Disney Concert Hall.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) and same 1984 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' listing as Park Güell.
Catenary/compression structural logic shared with Park Güell's viaducts and Laundry Room Portico, though executed as brick vaulting here (in the Espai Gaudí attic) versus stone columns there.

sheets.name: Espai Gaudí attic (catenary/parabolic brick arches)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (arches marked on site by builder Bayó and foreman Canaleta)
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase, as the attic laundry/drying space beneath the roof.
sheets.inspiration: The rippling roofline is widely compared to the ribs of a huge animal or the fronds of a palm; the space, now called Espai Gaudí, is often described as feeling like walking through the inside of a whale's ribcage.
sheets.purpose: The attic was built as the building's shared laundry and drying floor, and its arches carry the undulating roof and rooftop terrace above the apartments. It now houses the Espai Gaudí exhibition on Gaudí's work.
sheets.construction_process: Each arch's profile was set on site with a hanging-chain (catenary) model: nails were driven at the two spring points of the arch, a chain hung between them so its lowest point matched the desired deflection, and that traced curve became the template for the brick vault -- the same method Gaudí used at Casa Batlló and, earlier, on the roof of the Mataró workers' cooperative ('L'Obrera Mataronense').
technical_facts: Built using volta catalana (Catalan/timbrel vault) technique -- thin layered brick vaulting imported from Italy in the 14th century, laid without a full wooden centering framework.

Arch height and spacing directly follow the courtyards' footprint below: arches rise higher where the plan narrows and drop lower where it widens, so the roof structure encloses the irregular figure-8 courtyard shape beneath it.
artistic_facts: 270 parabolic brick arches of varying height, spaced about 80 cm apart, give the roofline a rippling, organic silhouette.
similarities: Same catenary/inverted-arch compression principle as Park Güell's viaducts and Laundry Room Portico, executed here in brick vaulting rather than stone columns.

Same catenary-model construction method (a hanging chain traced into a template) behind the self-supporting facade of this building, and directly comparable to the attic of Casa Batlló, also built by Gaudí with catenary brick arches.

sheets.name: Chimneys and rooftop sculptures ('caps')
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built as part of the roof during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; later restored to remove post-Gaudí chimneys, TV antennas, and other later additions.
sheets.inspiration: Nicknamed the 'garden of warriors' by poet Pere Gimferrer, since the grouped chimneys look like helmeted sentinels standing guard over the skylight/staircase exits; their helmet-like silhouettes are sometimes linked to Gaudí's interest in medieval fortress architecture.
sheets.purpose: Every piece on the roof does a job: the chimneys extract smoke from the apartments below, the vents renew the building's air, the discharge domes handle drainage, the skylight towers are the exits of the staircases, and some of those towers also house the water tanks. Their sculptural treatment is applied to elements that are functional first.
sheets.construction_process: Built from brick and coated with lime, broken marble, or glass; all pieces are functional (smoke extraction, ventilation, drainage) rather than purely decorative, despite their sculptural appearance.
technical_facts: The roof holds 28 chimneys in several groupings, 6 skylight/staircase exits, 2 half-hidden vents that renew air inside the building, and 4 discharge domes -- all functional rather than purely decorative.
Some staircase-exit towers double as housings for the building's water tanks, a few of which are snail-shaped.

The rooftop underwent a later restoration that removed chimneys added after Gaudí's death, TV antennas, and other additions, to return the roofscape closer to its originally designed functional layout.
artistic_facts: One chimney is topped with glass -- reportedly added by Gaudí the day after the building's inauguration party using empty champagne bottles, later restored with early-20th-century champagne-bottle bases.
similarities: Trencadís-style broken-tile cladding shared with the dragon and the serpentine bench at Park Güell.

sheets.name: Self-supporting stone facade
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; restored from 1987 onward, including rejoining fallen stone pieces sourced from the Villefranche quarry.
sheets.inspiration: Viewed from outside, the building reads in three parts: the main six-storey block with winding stone floors, two set-back floors with a smoother, whiter, wave-like curve, and the body of the roof.
sheets.purpose: The facade carries only its own weight, so it works as a self-supporting envelope rather than as structure: with the loads taken by the iron beams behind it, the front can open into large windows and balconies and the interior partitions can be moved freely without touching the building's stability.
sheets.construction_process: Large limestone blocks were cut to follow the projection of Gaudí's model, then raised into place and adjusted to align in a continuous curve with the surrounding pieces; the facade connects to curved iron floor beams rather than load-bearing walls.
technical_facts: Self-supporting: free of load-bearing walls, with the facade connected to curved iron beams around the perimeter of each floor, allowing large window openings and free interior layouts.
Original lower-level wrought ironwork was removed in 1928 when a tailor's shop opened in the building; one surviving balcony grille was later donated to MoMA, where it is on display.
artistic_facts: The undulating, rough-hewn stone facade and twisting wrought-iron balconies were controversial when built, giving rise to the 'La Pedrera' (stone quarry) nickname.
similarities: Structural principle (a self-supporting, non-load-bearing facade) distinct from but complementary to the compression-arch roof structure of the Espai Gaudí attic in the same building.
_notes: Check: the three landmark folders facana_1 / facana_2 / facana_3 for Casa Milà have all been mapped to this single sheet, as they are three views of the same facade.

sheets.name: Courtyards and interior gate
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (courtyard structure); wrought-iron gate design attributed to Josep Maria Jujol
sheets.timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase.
sheets.inspiration: The floor-support beam structure was interpreted by Josep Maria Carandell, who built the centerpiece at a shipyard, as representing the helm of a ship -- 'the soul of the building,' with a resemblance to Gothic crypts. The iron entrance gate's non-symmetrical structure evokes soap bubbles formed between the hands, or the structure of a plant cell.
sheets.purpose: The two courtyards exist to bring daylight and ventilation down to the nine storeys of apartments that have no street frontage. The wrought-iron gate was the building's entrance for both people and cars, giving access to the basement garage that is now an auditorium.
sheets.construction_process: Two courtyards (facing Passeig de Gràcia and Carrer de Provença) provide light to the building's nine stories; their floors are supported by cast-iron pillars, with two concentric cylindrical beams and stretched radial beams (like bicycle spokes) forming a central girder that works in tension and compression simultaneously.
technical_facts: The courtyard floor's central support girder combines two concentric cylindrical beams with stretched radial beams, functioning as a keystone working in both tension and compression -- structurally described as 'the soul of the building.'
The interior iron gate originally served both pedestrians and cars, providing access to the basement garage (now an auditorium).
artistic_facts: The two entrance halls are fully polychrome, with oil paintings on the plaster surfaces referencing mythology and flowers.
similarities: Wrought-iron gate design attributed to Jujol, like the trencadís serpentine bench at Park Güell.

sheets.name: Sagrada Família
aliases: Basílica i Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família
Temple Expiatori de la Sagrada Família
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (architect from 1883); begun by Francisco de Paula del Villar; driven by the bookseller José María Bocabella
sheets.timeline: Begun on 19 March 1882 under Villar (a neo-Gothic design); Gaudí took over in 1883 and radically transformed it; work was interrupted and the plans partly destroyed in the Civil War (1936); resumed from reconstructed plans in 1940; consecrated as a basilica by Pope Benedict XVI on 7 November 2010; the Nativity facade and the crypt were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005; the Tower of Jesus Christ was structurally completed on 20 February 2026 and inaugurated by Pope Leo XIV on 10 June 2026.
sheets.inspiration: Conceived as an 'expiatory temple' funded only by private donations, inspired by the basilica of Loreto after Bocabella's 1872 trip to the Vatican; it combines Gothic forms with Gaudí's own curvilinear Art Nouveau.
materials: stone from the Withnell quarry, England (from 2018)
sheets.construction_process: The crypt was begun by Villar in a standard neo-Gothic style; Gaudí redesigned the whole from 1883; construction was slow and funded only by donations; a fire in 1936 destroyed part of the workshops and the original plans, later reconstructed from photographs and documentation; computer-aided design (CAD/CNC) has been used since the 1980s, accelerating the pace of work.
technical_facts: The interior columns are a design unique to Gaudí: their cross-section passes from square to octagonal, then sixteen-sided and finally circular, through the intersection of helicoidal columns.
The Passion facade contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), in which the rows and columns add up to 33.
The Tower of Jesus Christ was deliberately designed one metre lower than the hill of Montjuïc, because Gaudí believed his work should not surpass God's.
artistic_facts: The temple has three great facades: the Nativity (the most ornate, finished before 1936), the Passion (austere and hard-lined, sculpted by Josep Maria Subirachs) and the Glory (the largest, still incomplete).
The spires represent, in ascending order of height, the Twelve Apostles, the four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and, tallest of all, Jesus Christ.
general_knowledge_facts: Stylistically compared to Spanish late Gothic, Catalan Modernisme and Art Nouveau; critics such as Louis Sullivan and Walter Gropius praised it, while George Orwell called it one of the ugliest buildings in the world -- matters of aesthetic opinion, not verifiable fact.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and Casa Batlló; only partly covered (the crypt and the Nativity facade) by the 2005 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' inscription -- unlike Park Güell and Casa Milà, which were listed in full in 1984.

sheets.name: Crossing Vaults and the Tower of Jesus Christ
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: The central nave vault was completed in 2000; the crossing structure and its great hyperboloid have been under construction since the early 2000s; the Tower of Jesus Christ was structurally completed on 20 February 2026.
sheets.inspiration: Gaudí wanted a visitor standing at the main entrance to see the nave, crossing and apse vaults rising in ascending perspective.
sheets.construction_process: The crossing rests on four central porphyry columns carrying one great hyperboloid, ringed by two circles of twelve smaller hyperboloids.
technical_facts: Hyperboloid forms become more pronounced in Gaudí's later design work, particularly from 1914 onwards.
artistic_facts: At 172.5 m, the Tower of Jesus Christ made the Sagrada Família the tallest church in the world, 11 m above the previous record holder, Ulm Minster.

sheets.name: Nativity Facade
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Built between 1893 and 1936, before work was interrupted by the Civil War; it is the oldest facade and the one most directly shaped by Gaudí. Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005 together with the crypt.
sheets.inspiration: Dedicated to the birth of Jesus; it faces north-east, towards the rising sun, as a symbol of Christ's birth. Gaudí chose to build it first because he considered it the most attractive and approachable for the public.
sheets.construction_process: Divided into three porticos dedicated to the theological virtues (Hope, Faith and Charity); crowned by four spires dedicated to the apostles Matthias, Barnabas, Jude Thaddaeus and Simon the Zealot.
artistic_facts: At the foot of each of the great pillars separating the porticos sits a tortoise (one land, one sea), a symbol of unchanging time; two chameleons at the sides symbolise change.
The Tree of Life rises above the door of Jesus, in the portico of Charity.
Gaudí wanted the whole facade polychromed, every archivolt and figure painted, so the figures would look as alive as the plants and animals depicted.
similarities: A deliberate contrast with the Passion facade: Gaudí explained that starting with a facade as hard and bony as the Passion would have driven the public away.

sheets.name: Passion Facade
sheets.creator: Designed by Antoni Gaudí (plans and instructions left for future architects); sculptures by Josep Maria Subirachs
sheets.timeline: Built to the design Gaudí left in 1917; work began in 1954; the spires were finished in 1976; Subirachs began the sculptural work in 1987.
sheets.inspiration: Dedicated to the Passion and death of Christ, facing west (the setting sun, a symbol of Christ's death); Gaudí wanted it to frighten those who looked at it, with 'broken' arches, 'cut' columns and strong chiaroscuro.
materials: bare stone, carved in straight, angular lines
sheets.construction_process: Supported by six great inclined columns evoking muscles under tension; crowned by a pyramidal pinnacle of eighteen bone-shaped columns topped by a large cross with a crown of thorns.
technical_facts: It contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), altered so that the rows and columns add up to 33 instead of 34.
artistic_facts: The scenes are arranged on three ascending levels in an S shape that follows the Stations of the Cross: the Last Supper and the kiss of Judas at the bottom, Calvary in the middle, and the Death, Burial and Resurrection at the top.
Each of the four spires is dedicated to an apostle (James, Thomas, Philip and Bartholomew).
general_knowledge_facts: Subirachs's angular, skeletal sculptures were controversial for their stylistic break with the rest of the building, though they follow the instructions Gaudí left.
similarities: A deliberate contrast with the Nativity facade on the same building.

sheets.name: Side Aisles and Lateral Naves
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: The double side-aisle structure is part of the temple's original plan.
sheets.inspiration: The floor plan -- double side aisles, an ambulatory and a chevet of seven apsidal chapels -- recalls historic Spanish cathedrals such as Burgos, León and Seville, though without right angles and with almost no straight lines.
sheets.construction_process: An unusual covered cloister encloses the temple in a rectangle, passing through the narthex of each of the three main porticos.
technical_facts: The apse columns, resting on Villar's foundations, do not follow the general grid, forcing a transition in the ambulatory that produces a horseshoe arrangement.

sheets.name: Apse (rear facade)
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (design influenced by Villar's original crypt)
sheets.timeline: Based on Villar's original crypt (1882-1883), redesigned by Gaudí from 1883 onwards.
sheets.inspiration: The apse, covered by a hyperboloid vault, completes the ascending sequence of vaults (nave, crossing, apse) that Gaudí wanted visible from the main entrance.
sheets.construction_process: Surrounded by a chevet of seven apsidal chapels.
technical_facts: Openings in the apse floor let visitors see down into the crypt below, where Gaudí is buried.
artistic_facts: The apse spire is engraved with the text of the Ave Maria in Latin.

sheets.name: Spires and Towers
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: The Nativity facade spires were finished around 1930; those of the Passion facade in 1976; the Tower of Jesus Christ was structurally completed on 20 February 2026.
sheets.inspiration: Eighteen spires are planned, in ascending order of height: the Twelve Apostles, the four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and, tallest of all, Jesus Christ.
sheets.construction_process: The Evangelists' spires are crowned by sculptures of their traditional symbols: a winged bull (St Luke), a winged man (St Matthew), an eagle (St John) and a winged lion (St Mark). Tubular bells, moved by the wind, are planned inside them.
technical_facts: The finials of the lower spires depict hosts with ears of wheat and chalices with bunches of grapes, Eucharistic symbols.
On 29 November 2021 an illuminated twelve-pointed glass star, 7 m across, was installed on the tower dedicated to the Virgin Mary.
artistic_facts: The geometric finials of the Nativity facade spires recall Cubism, though Gaudí's style drew on nature rather than on other artistic movements.

sheets.name: Casa Batlló
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí (the 1904-1906 remodelling, with Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, Josep Canaleta and Joan Rubió); original building by Emili Sala Cortés (1877); commissioned by Josep Batlló i Casanovas
sheets.timeline: The original building was built in 1877 for Lluís Sala Sánchez; bought by the Batlló family in 1903; Gaudí was hired in 1904 and the work finished in 1906; sold to the insurer Seguros Iberia in 1954; the outer balconies were restored in 1983 and the facade lit in 1984; bought by the Bernat family (Chupa Chups) in 1993; the noble floor opened to the public in 2002; declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
sheets.inspiration: Commissioned at the height of the rivalry between the bourgeois families of Passeig de Gràcia (the 'Illa de la Discòrdia', the Block of Discord): the textile industrialist Josep Batlló wanted a house that would put the neighbouring buildings by Puig i Cadafalch and Domènech i Montaner in their place.
sheets.purpose: A remodelling rather than a new build: Josep Batlló wanted the 1877 apartment block turned into a home for his family on the noble floor with rental flats above, and into a showpiece that would outshine its neighbours on the Illa de la Discòrdia. It has been open to the public as a house-museum since 2002.
sheets.construction_process: Not a new build but a remodelling: Gaudí persuaded Batlló not to demolish the 1877 building and to transform it instead; the central light well was enlarged and new floors added.
technical_facts: The attic has sixty catenary arches, creating a space that evokes the ribcage of an animal.
The central light well is clad in tiles in graded shades of blue (deeper at the top, lighter at the bottom) to spread light evenly between floors.
artistic_facts: Its popular name 'Casa dels Ossos' (House of Bones) comes from its biomorphic, skeletal look.
The arched roofline evokes the back of a dragon or dinosaur; a common reading casts the cross-topped tower as the lance of Saint George driven into the beast's back.
general_knowledge_facts: There is a popular legend, unconfirmed by documentary sources, that the Sagrada Família (then under construction) could once be seen through the small triangular window in the roof; in 2022 it was confirmed that the towers are partly visible from that point today.
similarities: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and the Sagrada Família; part of the Illa de la Discòrdia alongside other notable Modernista buildings (not by Gaudí).
Trencadís used here as on the Park Güell dragon, the serpentine bench and the Casa Milà rooftop chimneys.
Catenary arches in the attic -- the same construction technique as the Espai Gaudí attic at Casa Milà.

sheets.name: Main Facade
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Remodelled between 1904 and 1906.
sheets.inspiration: The central section evokes the surface of a lake with water lilies, recalling Monet's Water Lilies, through the rippling effect of the glass and ceramic mosaic.
sheets.purpose: The street facade is the building's public face, the part that had to win the rivalry of the Illa de la Discòrdia, and it works as display as much as enclosure. It is also functional: the galleries and balconies light and ventilate the front rooms, and the upper crown is a gable built to hide the old water tank.
materials: Montjuïc sandstone (ground floor and first-floor galleries)
sheets.construction_process: The facade divides into three integrated sections: the ground floor and galleries in undulating sandstone, the multicoloured central part with its balconies, and the upper crown, a great gable that conceals the old water tank.
technical_facts: The upper crown carries a frieze of ceramic pieces open to various readings; Gaudí reused trencadís fragments left over from other works.
artistic_facts: The metallic-finish roof tiles mimic the scales of a monster, shading from green (where the head begins) to blue and violet in the centre, and to red and pink at the far left.
The tower is topped by a four-armed cross facing the cardinal points and carries the monograms of Jesus (JHS), Mary (M with a ducal crown) and Joseph (JHP) in gilded ceramic.
A small triangular window in the roof stands for the dragon's eye.
similarities: Shares the trencadís technique with other Gaudí works at Park Güell and Casa Milà.

sheets.name: Ground Floor and Noble Floor
sheets.creator: Antoni Gaudí
sheets.timeline: Remodelled between 1904 and 1906; opened to the public as a museum in 2002 (the noble floor) and extended to the attic and light well in 2004.
sheets.inspiration: The ground floor is the most striking part of the building, with unusual tracery, irregular oval windows and stone carved into sinuous shapes, almost without straight lines.
sheets.purpose: The ground floor holds the entrance and the private hall that leads up to the noble floor; the noble floor itself was the Batlló family's own home, laid out as living rooms, Batlló's study and a dining room. Both levels are now the main route of the house-museum, open to visitors since 2002.
sheets.construction_process: The noble floor is reached through a private hall with tortoise-shell skylights and curved vaulted walls; it includes Batlló's study, a dining room and a corner reserved for couples, with a mushroom-shaped fireplace.
technical_facts: The rounded openings and lip-like carved edges give the ground floor its nickname 'casa dels badalls' (the house of yawns).
artistic_facts: Six slender columns in front of the large windows suggest the bones of a limb with a central joint, though they are in fact floral decoration.
